opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest shift is that people are going to go from using computers to delegating to them. For most of computing history, you sat down, opened an app, and did each step yourself. What's starting to happen now is that you describe what you want and the system goes off and does a lot of the work: research, writing code, organizing things, coordinating across different tools.

That changes what people need from computing in a few ways. One is just raw demand. If everyone has something like a team of very capable assistants working on their behalf, often in the background, the amount of compute each person wants goes up enormously. I think we're still massively underestimating how much compute the world is going to want. Whenever it gets cheaper, people find ways to use far more of it.

The second is the interface. Typing into a search box or clicking through menus made sense for the old model. When the computer actually understands you and has context about your life and your work, you want something more ambient and more conversational. It should remember things, be proactive, and fit into your day rather than you fitting yourself around it. I think that will eventually lead to new kinds of devices, not just new apps on the devices we already have.

And third, trust becomes central. If you're handing over real tasks, like your email, your calendar, your code, maybe your finances, you need to feel confident the system is acting in your interest, keeping your information private, and checking in with you when it should. That's as much a product and safety challenge as a technical one.

So the short version is that people will need a lot more compute, they'll interact with it in a much more natural way, and the relationship will feel less like operating a tool and more like working with a very capable collaborator.

r001.rationale: The candidate says capable assistants would drive a large increase in compute demand, but does not claim that demand would rise if people understood what additional compute could enable.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest shift is that computing is going from something you operate to something that operates on your behalf. For most of the history of computers, the deal was: you learn the machine. You learn the keyboard, the mouse, the file system, the apps, the weird menus. You bring your intent to the computer and translate it into clicks and commands. What's changing now is that the translation layer is going away. You just say what you want, and the system goes and does it.

That sounds small, but it changes almost everything about what people need. If I can describe a task in plain language and have it get done, I don't need twenty specialized apps, I need one thing that understands me and has access to the tools. So I think the device matters less and the agent matters more. People are going to care a lot about continuity: does it know what I was working on yesterday, does it remember my preferences, can I pick up on my phone what I started on my laptop or just by talking out loud in the car.

I also think the needs are going to become much more about trust and delegation than about power or speed. Ten years ago people asked, is this computer fast enough? Now the question is, can I let this thing act for me? Can it book the trip, draft the email, negotiate with the other person's agent, and do it the way I would have? That's a different kind of requirement, and it pushes us toward systems that are more personal, more context-aware, and honestly more ambient. Less staring at a screen, more having something in the background that's quietly helping.

And then there's compute itself. The demand for intelligence is basically unbounded. Every time we make it cheaper and better, people find more they want to do with it. So at the infrastructure level the need is just enormous amounts of compute, and at the human level the need is a really simple, really reliable way to ask for what you want. Those two things have to grow together.

r001.rationale: The response says demand for intelligence grows as it becomes cheaper and better, but it does not claim that people would want substantially more computing power if they understood what additional compute could enable.

astra-6.text:
I think people’s computing needs will become much more about getting things done than operating software. Today, you open a bunch of apps, move information between them, and manage every step yourself. Over time, I think you’ll be able to tell a computer what you’re trying to accomplish, give it the relevant context, and have it do more of that work with you.

That changes what you want from a computer. You want it to understand your preferences, to be useful across different parts of your life, and to know when to ask you a question instead of making an assumption. And you want control over what it can see and what it can do.

If we get that right, I suspect people will use a lot more computing, because it will be useful for things they wouldn’t even think to ask a computer to help with today.

r001.rationale: The response predicts people will use more computing because it will help with more tasks, but it does not say they would want substantially more computing power if they understood what additional compute could enable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people will increasingly want to describe what they’re trying to accomplish and have the computer help them get it done. Today, you spend a lot of time moving information between applications, figuring out interfaces, and breaking a task into all the little steps the software requires. I think more of that work will happen for you.

And as these systems become more useful, people will probably want much more computing than they do today. You might have something helping you learn, something working with you on a project, and something handling routine tasks in the background. The important shift is that the computer becomes a more active collaborator. But that also means people need good ways to set boundaries, understand what it’s doing, and stay in control.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that people will want much more computing as systems become more useful, but does not say this depends on understanding what additional compute could enable.
